articles.text: Russian scholar Anastasia Edel returns to the Forum this winter presented by Healdsburg American Association of University Women for an in-depth look into Russia’s war on Ukraine. She will lead a six-part class on Thursdays from February 2 to March 9. Starting on the day when Russian missiles first struck cities across the sovereign nation of Ukraine, Edel will tackle the key questions: Why did Russia become an aggressor bent on destroying a neighboring nation with whom it shares centuries of common heritage? How did it happen? Why does Putin’s regime refuse to call the war “war”? What’s behind Ukrainians’ resilience and Russians’ acquiescence? And how does this all end for Russia, Ukraine, and the world? articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont hosted a Zoom event on January 18 entitled “Sustainable Groundwater in California: The Challenges Ahead”. The discussion featured Tim Godwin, Technical Policy Advisor for Sustainable Groundwater, who filled in for the scheduled speaker, Paul Gosselin, Deputy Director of Sustainable Groundwater for the State Department of Water Resources, who had a last-minute Godwin spoke in detail about the requirements and mechanics of the Sustainable Groundwater Act (SGMA), the first California law to regulate groundwater. SGMA became law in 2014. In times of drought, groundwater supplies up to 60% of the State’s total water needs. Even in wetter years, groundwater can account for 40% of total state usage. Some basins are 100% dependent on groundwater. SGMA implementation is envisaged over a 20-year period. It enables the formation of local Groundwater Sustainability Agencies (GSAs), which oversee basins in their areas. Of more than 500 alluvial basins, SGMA has identified 21 that are critically overdrafted. An additional 94, representing 90% of total groundwater pumping in California, are considered high and medium priority. Currently, plans for eight of the 21 critical overdraft basins have been approved. SGMA defines sustainability in terms of six conditions to be avoided: 1) lowering groundwater levels 2) reduction of groundwater storage 3) seawater intrusion 4) degraded water quality 5) land subsidence 6) depletion of interconnected streams As an example of land subsidence, Godwin told of the Friant-Kern Canal, which has had a 60% reduction in its ability to convey water, due to the partial collapse of land subsidence. He noted that when land above an aquifer starts to collapse, it threatens bridges, railways, pipelines and water pipes. Godwin explained that determining the appropriate metrics for groundwater pumping, water levels and recharge is a complex process. Each local agency needs to evaluate the level of demand for water, sources of supply, risk of contamination, performance of local wells, and many other factors. To learn more about this talk and see the presentation, visit the League’s website at www. lwvpiedmont.org. To view a recording, visit the League’s YouTube channel at https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC3v60XGmr13V_9WaYj6qUJg.

articles.text: Is your New Year’s resolution to read more? Maybe you want to learn more about climate science. Here is a list of engaging books about climate change. Some will leave you hopeful for the future while others are a stark reminder of what’s at stake if we don’t address the climate crisis. The list also includes a novel that tackles environmental issues. 1. All We Can Save: Truth, Courage, and Solutions for the Climate Crisis, Edited by Ayana Elizabeth Johnson and Katharine K. Wilkinson “All We Can Save illuminates the insights of dozens of diverse women leading on climate in the United States . The list includes scientists, journalists, farmers, lawyers, teachers, activists, innovators, wonks, and designers across generations, geographies, and race. It aims to advance a more representative, nuanced, and solution-oriented public conversation on the climate crisis. These women offer a spectrum of ideas and insights for how we can rapidly, radically reshape society.” 2. Braiding Sweetgrass by Robin Wall Kimmerer “Drawing on her life as an indigenous scientist, a mother, and a woman, Kimmerer shows how other living beings – asters and goldenrod, strawberries and squash, salamanders, algae, and sweetgrass – offer us gifts and lessons, even if we’ve forgotten how to hear their voices. In a rich braid of reflections that range from the creation of Turtle Island to the forces that threaten its flourishing today, she circles toward a central argument: that the awakening of a wider ecological consciousness requires the acknowledgment and celebration of our reciprocal relationship with the rest of the living world.” 3. The Day the World Stops Shopping: How Ending Consumerism Saves the Environment and Ourselves by J.B. MacKinnon “Consuming less is our best strategy for saving the planet — but can we do it? In this thoughtful and surprisingly optimistic book, journalist J. B. MacKinnon investigates how we may achieve a world without shopping. Drawing from experts in fields ranging from climate change to economics, MacKinnon investigates how living with less would change our planet, our society, and ourselves. Along the way, he reveals just how much we stand to gain: an investment in our physical and emotional wellness. The pleasure of caring for our possessions. Closer relationships with our natural world and one another. Imaginative and inspiring, The Day the World Stops Shopping will embolden you to envision another way.” 4. Climate Change is Racist: Race Privilege and the Struggle for Climate Justice by Jeremy Williams “In this eye-opening book, writer and environmental activist Jeremy Williams takes us on a short, urgent journey across the globe – from Kenya to India, the USA to Australia – to understand how White privilege and climate change overlap. We’ll look at the environmental facts, hear the experiences of the people most affected on our planet and learn from the activists leading the change.” “That bridge you said we would cross when we came to it? Well, we’ve come to it.”
articles.title: Environmental books to read in 2023

articles.text: Piedmont resident Rupa Basu to address health impacts from rising temperatures Pied mont Con nect and the League of Women Voters (LWV) of Piedmont continue their 2022-23 Climate Speaker Series on Wednesday, February 8, from 4:00 to 5:00 p.m. with an online presentation by Piedmont resident Dr. Rupa Basu. The talk will highlight the health impacts of fossil-fuel pollution presenting the latest scientific evidence, followed by a live, moderated Q&A. pages.text: Wednesday, January 25, 2023 3 LWV hosts discussion on Sustainable Groundwater By Jennifer Trainor The League of Women Voters of Piedmont hosted a Zoom event on January 18 entitled “Sustainable Groundwater in California: The Challenges Ahead”. The discussion featured Tim Godwin, Technical Policy Advisor for Sustainable Groundwater, who filled in for the scheduled speaker, Paul Gosselin, Deputy Director of Sustainable Groundwater for the State Department of Water Resources, who had a last-minute emergency. Godwin spoke in detail about the requirements and mechanics of the Sustainable Groundwater Act (SGMA), the first California law to regulate groundwater. SGMA became law in 2014. In times of drought, groundwater supplies up to 60% of the State’s total water needs. Even in wetter years, groundwater can account for 40% of total state usage. Some basins are 100% dependent on groundwater. SGMA implementation is envisaged over a 20-year period. It enables the formation of local Groundwater Sustainability Agencies (GSAs), which oversee basins in their areas. Of more than 500 alluvial basins, SGMA has identified 21 that are critically overdrafted. An additional 94, representing 90% of total groundwater pumping in California, are considered high and medium priority. Currently, plans for eight of the 21 critical overdraft basins have been approved. SGMA defines sustainability in terms of six conditions to be avoided: 1) lowering groundwater levels 2) reduction of groundwater storage 3) seawater intrusion 4) degraded water quality 5) land subsidence 6) depletion of interconnected streams As an example of land subsidence, Godwin told of the Friant-Kern Canal, which has had a 60% reduction in its ability to convey water, due to the partial collapse of land subsidence. He noted that when land above an aquifer starts to collapse, it threatens bridges, railways, pipelines and water pipes. Godwin explained that determining the appropriate metrics for groundwater pumping, water levels and recharge is a complex process. Each local agency needs to evaluate the level of demand for water, sources of supply, risk of contamination, performance of local wells, and many other factors. articles.text: On January 17, City Council unanimously voted to issue a request for proposals (RFP) to seek a consultant for the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. The Plan, which is part of Piedmont’s draft 6th Cycle Housing Element, aims to improve existing facilities and incorporate 132 units of housing on 18 acres of city-owned land on both sides of Moraga Canyon, along Moraga Avenue; 60 units of this housing would be available to lower-income households. The land affected by the Moraga Canyon Plan includes Blair Park, Coaches Field, Kennelly Skate Park, and the Corporation Yard. The RFP outlines the requirements for a prospective consultant’s analysis of this plan. Planning Director Kevin Jackson said that the city will “engage professional services … and begin the planning process” by April. Jackson emphasized the three most significant requirements of the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan as identified by the RFP: “a robust public engagement program … [the determination of] a site for the development of at least one affordable housing project … [and] a fiscal analysis of potential revenues and expenses.” City Administrator Sara Lillevand said that she expected these public engagement methods — ranging from “online activities, mapping tools … to scoping meetings with neighbors and experts, to … meetings with City Council [and] Commissions” — to be “a lot more fun than our Housing Element,” because Piedmonters “know Moraga Canyon. They drive it, or live there … it’s much more tangible. And people understand what they think should happen there. I think it’s going to be much easier to get people engaged here.” Due largely to the fact that much Housing Element public engagement was remote during the pandemic, Jackson said that Moraga Canyon outreach will be more hands-on and more similar to community meeting about the new Piedmont Community Pool. “People will get to think about the space in a geometric way,” he said. The identification of a possible affordable housing site will take priority in these discussions, said Jackson, as this site must qualify for the $2.2 million allocated to Piedmont by Alameda County through its Measure A1 low-interest loan program for affordable housing development. Piedmont will seek the County’s approval for this loan funding by 2024. While the RFP does not set a price for the Moraga Canyon plan altogether, Lillevand said that, per a study published by the Association of Bay Area Governments in 2019, “the preparation of a specific plan cost an average of $544,237,” and that the city expects a similar price. The Moraga Plan will be funded by the General Plan Maintenance Fee collected from building permit applications and instituted in Piedmont on July 1, 2019. Last year, this fee generated $427,000. Although similar revenue is expected this year, Jackson said that the city has already spent much of the fee on expenses incurred through the Housing Element drafting process. Given that the Moraga Plan is what councilmember Tom Ramsey called “a non-funded state mandate,” the city is investigating state grants to recoup costs not covered by the Maintenance Fee. The RFP city staff report states that “the most promising [funding source] may be a Priority Development Area Planning Grant from MTC [Metropolitan Transportation Commission]. However Piedmont has no Priority Development Areas – which are “generally tied to major transit facilities like a BART station or ferry stop or the intersection of several bus lines,” explained Jackson. Nevertheless, the state is seeking to create new Priority Development Area categories which increase transportation mobility. Jackson told Council that the city has already begun working to identify Moraga Canyon as such an area, and possibly apply for the grant this way. The RFP staff report is available at bit.ly/3ZR5RLn. Those with questions about the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan can contact Planning and Building Director Kevin Jackson by email at kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3039.

articles.text: Planning Director Kevin Jackson told City Council that the city expects to adopt the Element before the state deadline, January 31, and before it receives a letter of compliance from the state. City Council will hold a special meeting on January 30 to consider adopting the 2023-2031 6th Cycle Housing Element. In a special meeting on January 12, the Planning Commission voted unanimously to recommend to the Council that it adopt the Element. Because cities which do not adopt an Element by the deadline face penalties from the state, Piedmont is expected to adopt the plan even if it does not receive comments by then from the California Department of Housing and Community Development, confirming that the Element complies with state standards. Piedmont submitted its Housing Element to the state on November 15. Because the HCD sets a 90-day review period before releasing comments regarding Housing Element compliance, the city expects to receive a letter from the state by February 16. Jackson stated that Piedmont would not be unique in adopting the Element before it is confirmed by the state: While “there are communities in southern California who are ahead of us in the phases of Housing Element adoption,” he said, “here in the Bay Area, particularly in Alameda County, most jurisdictions are planning to adopt prior to getting a letter of substantial compliance from HCD.” Furthermore, emphasized Jackson, city staff has already been communicating with the HCD to clarify the standards which Piedmont must meet and to ensure that the city does meet them. “In December and the first part of January,” he said, “city staff and our consultant have had a handful of virtual meetings with the HCD staff member assigned to review Piedmont’s Housing Element.” These meetings “enabled the reviewer to ask questions and make comments and for us to respond with answers and clarify how the Element complies with state law.” Jackson gave the HCD staff member assigned to Piedmont a tour of the city on January 13. “I didn’t get a lot of feedback; it was mostly me presenting the sites that we have [in the Element],” Jackson said that the tour nevertheless allowed the reviewer to confirm Piedmont’s compliance, site-by-site, against “a checklist of items of state law which we need to comply with.” Given that Housing Element compliance is a “much more cumbersome process than in prior cycles” due to “additional requirements of state law that the legislature has adopted in recent years,” Jackson told the Council that many cities in the Bay Area like Piedmont are finding it more efficient to adopt the Element and direct staff to “make changes that would bring our element into compliance” after comments are received, rather than withholding adoption before the state deadline and facing subsequent penalties. Information about the Housing Element update process is available at PiedmontIsHome. org. Those with questions about the Element can contact Jackson by email at kjackson@piedmont. ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3039.

articles.text: Raiyaan Shah (left), Jasper Tripp, Jasper Zietlow, Chelsea Yi, Gabi Kong, Zain Shah, Rahimeen Shah, and Derek Chan On Friday, January 20, a group of students from Piedmont High’s Asian Student Union (ASU) stayed after school to decorate the campus halls with handmade lanterns and gold streamers in preparation for the Lunar New Year for the Year of the Hare. It was only the fourth year of the decorating tradition. ASU is one of the high school’s many identity-oriented clubs, which gives students who lack representation within the student population a place to connect and build community. ASU spreads knowledge about different Asian cultures to the entire school, with decorations being one of the ways ASU can represent identities. With Kaeli Huh and Zoe Saldanha having graduated in 2022, senior Gabi Kong has picked up the reins this year as club president. Kong joined ASU as a freshman and immediately found value the club provides. “I think especially in Piedmont, where we’re a majority white community, it’s important to have these types of clubs like ASU and BSU (Black Student Union), the social justice clubs, and all the cultural clubs because it’s another doorway for representation,” said Kong. “It creates a safe space for these students who are a minority. They can feel like they are seen and heard through these communities.” Many students are grateful for the community the club has created. “I joined ASU just to celebrate Asian heritage and to hang out with other people that also have similar cultures and backgrounds,” said junior Derek Chan, who joined as a sophomore. While ASU is currently highSenior Jasper Zietlow hard at work lighting the Lunar New Year, a holiday most celebrated in East Asia, the club represents South Asians as well. “I joined ASU because I think that South Asians are quite underrepresented in our school,” explained Senior Rahimeen Shah. “I want to bring more attention to different things such as Eid, a Muslim holiday, which is not necessarily South Asian, but I feel like many people don’t know about it.” ASU has given many students a space to build bonds and celebrate their diverse backgrounds. At the beginning of the new year ASU hopped into action by working on a new student social justice project to create systemic change, started by PUSD DEI director Dr. Marguerite Vanden Wyngaard. Faculty Advisor Shelley Seto (left), with members of Piedmont’s Asian Student Union Gabi Kong, Madelyn Hill, and Chelsea Yi. Derek Chan hangs up a string of lanterns in the background. articles.text: NASA built a test to measure “creative genius” by looking for high levels of divergent thinking, a thought process that tackles problems using innovative approaches. It’s pretty important when your line of work is hurtling rockets into space. This test was simple enough that a child could take it, and so, NASA administered the test to 1600 five-yearolds. The result? Ninety-eight percent tested within the bounds of “creative genius”. NASA decided to test the same children again five years later. Only 30% of the now 10--yearolds were considered to have creative-genius-level thinking. Fast forward five more years and the number dropped to 12%. The final test, conducted after another five years, resulted in only 2% of adults testing within genius level divergent thinking. What happened to those children’s creativity over the years? The general consensus is that school happened. Instead of favoring open-ended divergent thinking, evaluative and judgment-oriented convergent thinking was rewarded and prioritized. “Two plus two is four” and “W-O-R-D spells word” are examples of convergent thinking, which favors facts with right and wrong answers. Unfortunately, most schools do not offer spaces and Children utilize divergent thinking throughout their time at summer camp. lessons for divergent thinking to thrive alongside analytical thinking, which may explain how we lost 96% of our creative geniuses. The good news is that we don’t need to sit around twiddling our thumbs waiting for schools to change. Creative thinking can be nurtured and strengthened with a little practice. Expanding our divergent minds can be as simple as coming up with as many uses for a paperclip as possible, or considering all the ways a common fork could be improved. For children, summer camp can be an extremely liberating experience after spending all year in a classroom. Free from outside influence and expectations, campers can pursue a week that is entirely their own. Part of the magic of summer camp lies in the truth: there is no right or wrong way to be. Summer camp staff can attest to having seen time and time again children expand in front of their eyes as they take on new activities, challenges, and identities. In truth, divergent thinking doesn’t make us rocket scientists, but it does help us imagine a better world. If children are the future, then right now a good many of them are still full-fledged creative geniuses. Let’s give them every shot at staying that way. Randall Grayson, PhD, is the Director of Camp Augusta, which sits nestled in the Sierra Nevada foothills near Nevada City and is beloved by Piedmont families since its founding by Edwin and Charlotte Ehmann in 1931. Information about the camp’s summer programs and family camps can be found at www.campaugusta.org.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. articles.text: Havens Dad Jimmy Lee won the 15th annual Havens Dads Club Poker Night tournament, on Friday, January 20, an event which raised an all-time record $48,328. Lee outlasted every other player in a field of 150 to take home the ultimate poker bragging rights and the championship bracelet. Dueling Lee at the final table after four hours of play were the top three runners-up, Brandon Bercovich, Stephanie Ho, and Barron Hong. The event, hosted by Dads Club President Roger Tsai and a team of 21 volunteer parents, was held at the Veterans Hall, and generated a crowd of 185 people for Havens School’s single largest fundraiser. Havens Principal Anne Dolid along with school board members and Havens staff Havens Parents Club President Katie Castles Shaffer (left) and Havens Principal Anne Dolid welcome the crowd to the annual Havens Dads Club Poker Night on January 20. The first card was dealt at 6:30 p.m. Friday night until the large field of 150 hopeful players dwindled down to one winner, Jimmy Lee. Piedmont Veterans Hall was filled with high rollers Friday night. cheered on the bettors. “We want our event to be representative of our community and everyone showed up in full support,” noted parent T.J. Won. “We also had many more women [as contestants] than before, a major goal for the event organizers.” The evening was a Texas Hold’em tournament costing $100 to join, with dozens of professional tables and dealers. Since all the proceeds go to the schools, when a player was knocked out, they had the option to get more chips for another $100, as many times as desired. “I usually have a pretty good strategy when playing small cash games for fun with friends; I play pretty conservative. You have to throw that all out the window with this fundraising event and the unlimited buy back. A guy at my table spent $4,000 a few years ago by constantly buying back in,” said Havens dad Jon Essner. Proceeds from the event will be used for Havens School projects, such as supplemental funding for the Becker Field replacement turf, Ellen Driscoll Playhouse mural repairs, lunch tables and awnings, and playground blocks. The event received sponsorship from Lisa Chan-Carnazzo of The Grubb Company, and Chris Kwei of Oakland Kia. articles.text: The Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Film Series returned to the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse on Thursday, January 19, for the screening of an engaging, powerful documentary, Through the Night. The film was followed by a remarkable and informative talk and Q & A. The film, a New York Times Critics Pick in 2020, showcases the multiplicity of “women’s work” – paid, underpaid, and unpaid – through a tender portrait of strength, love, and selflessness. This film is an intimate cinema verite portrait of working mothers whose lives intersect at a 24-hour daycare center: a mother working the overnight shift as an essential worker at a pediatric hospital, another holding three jobs to support her family, and an inspirational woman delivering exemplary 24-hour care and education for over two decades. Support for working mothers remains very limited across the country. The costs of daycare for a three-year-old rivals the cost of rent in most U.S. cities. Childcare providers themselves are often struggling in a mountain of expensive bureaucracy and minimum wages. The audience warmly received three speakers who followed the screening: Kym Johnson, Director of the acclaimed East Bay childcare referral and family resources center Bananas, and Nancy Harvey and Tasha Jordan, childcare providers. Johnson summarized local childcare needs and new state bills bringing some increased and sorely needed funding to Oakland. Harvey and Jordan of Oakland were able to explain the hardworking, caring network of childcare/early education first line workers who support families, especially when no other support exists. They announced that AB 378: Building a Better Early Care & Education Act, was signed by Governor Newsom and gives providers the right to form a union. Subsequently CCPU (Child Care Providers United: childcareprovidersunited.org) was formed and currently represents over 30,000 child care providers in California. Visit the Appreciating Diversity Film Series website (diversityfilmseries.org) to read its mission, its documentary film archive, and an opportunity to subscribe to its e-mail list to receive notices of all films scheduled this year.

articles.text: PHS girls topple O’Dowd. San Leandro; take aim on league title Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team continues to be regarded as one of the best in Northern California, and possibly in the state. During the past week they won four games all on the road, significantly including a 69-62 win against rival Bishop O’Dowd on Wednesday, January 18. They beat last year’s nemesis, San Leandro, 79-57 on Monday, January 23, bashed Berkeley 52-20, and outscored North Coast Section power Acalanes 66-51 at the Sabrina Ionescu 20 Showcase on Saturday, January 21. The result? The Highlanders remain on top of many lists with a sterling 19-0 record. Their win over O’Dowd marked the squad’s fourth consecutive victory over the Dragons going back to the spring of 2021, and puts them in control of the Western Alameda County Conference with a 5-0 league record. But it didn’t come without some drama. Piedmont hung onto a narrow lead late in the game after senior captain Trinity Zamora exited due to an injury with 3:19 remaining, followed by senior forward Eva Levingston who fouled out with 1:57 left. “Our main players got injured and it was a very intense game. We stayed composed and our mental toughness was there. We finished it out,” said junior guard Natalia Martinez, who led all scoring with 29 points, 17 of which came in the second half. Without Levingston and Zamora in the closing minutes, the game required a big contribution from point guard Perseas Gioukaris. The senior guard was dealing with leg cramps at the time Zamora left the game, but Staff Photos Maddie Hill was named MVP at the SI20 Showcase. Perseas Gioukaris converted a crucial 3-pointer in the closing minute to help Piedmont beat O’Dowd. Natalia Martinez led the scoring with 29 points in a critical win over Bishop O’Dowd. Gioukaris was able to persevere, With Piedmont leading 62-60 with less than under a minute left, Gioukaris knocked down a critical 3-pointer to put the dagger in the game. “Tri [Zamora] went down, so I knew I had to step up. I had Nat [Martinez] and Maddie [Hill] with me, we’re all great components and we work well together. Maddie drove to the basket, I had the open shot and I took it,” said Gioukaris recalling the play. 69-62 over Bishop O’Dowd Piedmont trailed in the early minutes against the Dragons, but regained the lead at 10-9 and never relinquished from then on, thought it sure got close. After leading 37-22 at halftime, the Highlanders begun getting into foul trouble. The Dragons inched away until closing the gap to five points to start the fourth quarter, 50-45. Clinging to a 60-55 lead, Piedmont’s Gioukaris suffered leg cramping followed by before Zamora suffering an injury that forced her out of the game. After a brief break, Gioukaris re-entered the game with 3:19 to play. Martinez sank a pair of free throws to make it 62-55, but Levingston fouled out with 1:57 left. O’Dowd then scored five straight points to cut Piedmont’s lead to 62-60, feeling that the momentum had shifted. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team improved its record to 5-4-2 (W-T-L) last week, defeating Tennyson 3-2 on Friday, January 20 at Witter Field and tying Alameda 1-1 on Wednesday, January 18 on the road. Both matches were with non-league Shoreline Division teams of the Western Alameda County Conference. Piedmont competes in the Foothill Division. PHS is unbeaten in its last five matches. Against Tennyson, the Highlanders controlled possession and were up 2-0 before relinquishing a goal minutes before halftime. Piedmont made it 3-1 in the early minutes of the second half and had several opportunities to extend the lead. However, the Lancers closed the final score to 3-2 with a penalty kick in second half stoppage time. “It was a bit of a disjointed start. Tennyson showed up 10 minutes before the game and I knew things would carry over into the game,” said coach Todd Sullivan. “We created chances but we never got going in terms of possession and quality. I think it’s very rare to see us play like that.” Sophomore forward Enzo Bernales currently leads the team in goals through 10 matches with four to his credit. He scored on a free kick from around 25 yards against Tennyson. He’s a firstyear starter this year and closed his freshman season with a few appearances on varsity. “It’s hard to step up after players like Andre Stankiewicz, Conner Curtis, and Ian Work leave from last year’s team. They were a huge part of this team. Practically everyone has to step up to fill their roles,” said Bernales. 3-2 win over Tennyson The Highlanders were on the offensive against Tennyson, recording three shots on target through the first 20 minutes but had a goal wiped out due to an offside call in the 16th minute. Piedmont’s first goal came in the 21st minute at the end of a corner lick when Evan Manolis’ connected with Sam Shelby for the goal. Bernales scored the next goal in the 34th minute after the Highlanders drew a foul about 25 yards out. Bernales rocketed in a low-bending shot for a 2-0 lead. Tennyson scored in the closing minute of the first half when playing a long ball to their striker, resulting in the athletic forward chipping the ball over Piedmont goalkeeper Brady Hinsch. Staff Photos Enzo Bernales scored on a nice free kick against Tennyson, his fourth goal of the season. Myles Gray scored against Tennyson and Alameda. He’s pictured here scoring a penalty kick as the Lancers’ players watch. In the second half, Piedmont was awarded a penalty kick when Jacques Saldanha drew contact in the area. Myles Gray stepped to the ball, slotting it home to put his team ahead 3-1. The Highlanders stayed on the attack, recording shots on target by Shelby, Bernales, and two by Jack Nelson. Int in the closing minutes of stoppage time, the Lancers were awarded a penalty after a long ball was played into the box—making it a 3-2 final. 1-1 draw with Alameda The Hornets took the lead moments before halftime after drawing a foul just inside Piedmont’s half. Alameda played their free kick into the area, leading to a header goal by the Hornets’ striker. Piedmont came out in its usual pressing style in the second half to close down passing lanes for Alameda and forcing them to run. It took a toll on the opposition, forcing a few players to the ground with leg cramps. Sullivan then subbed Andrew Szerdy into the attacking midfield role. Szerdy sent a pass into the area toward Gray, using his speed to beat a defender and score the 1-1 equalizer. From there, Piedmont had several opportunities to take the lead but were unable to find the finishing touch. They had at least three shots ring off of the post, while forcing multiple saves by the Alameda keeper. articles.text: Photo courtesy of Barstool Sports Mackie McDonald (right) exited the Australian Open in the third round, but only after pulling off the biggest win of his career over Rafael Nadal last week. Mackie McDonald put up a battle but lost in the third round of the Australian Open to No. 31 seed Yoshihito Nishioka on Thursday, January 19 in three sets, 7-6 (8-6), 6-3, 6-2. Regardless of the exit for McDonald, he walked out of the Grand Slam after pulling off the biggest win of his professional career when defeating Rafael Nadal in three sets a week ago on January 17. McDonald reflected on his win over Nadal and how the Spanish legend dealt with a nagging hip injury late in the match. “I’m really happy with how I started that match, I thought I was playing really well, serving great, and returning well too. I was really taking it to him. But I hated to see him (injured) in the third set. It was pretty tough to stay mentally engaged, but I just found a way to pull it out,” said McDonald. McDonald admitted that he got out of rhythm after Nadal suffered his injury. “He’s an incredible champion, he’s never going to give up regardless of the situation, so even closing it out against a top guy like that is always tough. I was trying to stay focused on what I was doing and he got me out of rhythm with that. I’m happy that I just kept focusing on myself in the end and got through,” said McDonald. Regardless of Nadal’s injury, McDonald played steady throughout the match and he’s aware just how on top of his game he was on that Wednesday morning in Melbourne. McDonald has always been best on the hard courts and feels he had the “guns” to keep up with the former champion. “I think I have the guns to do it. I was blasting the ball, hitting really flat. Last time I played him, he kicked my butt. On clay courts, it’s tough to hit through, but here I like my chances on hard courts. I really wanted to take it to him on a hard court, I happy I got that opportunity and got away with it,” said McDonald. Former Piedmont coach Neil Rothenberg, who coached McDonald when he was a student at Piedmont High School, made an appearance on ABC7 News to talk about Mackie. “It was awesome to watch it. You’re always on pins and needles, especially when you’re playing one of the greatest players of all time. After the first set, you always get nervous and ask ‘Can he win the second set?’ and then it became, ‘Well, can he actually win the match?’ He has a lot of fans in Piedmont, we were all communicating with each other,” said Rothenberg. “I don’t think I’ve ever seen him play as well as he did and I’ve known him since he was seven years old. He would go to some of the clinics that pros would hold and he was always involved as one of the participants. You could tell even at seven- and eight-years old that he had an unbelievable amount of presence. We were just hoping that when he got to high school that he would play for Piedmont because it’s very unusual to have a world class player play high school tennis,” said Rothenberg. We’ll cover McDonald once again in the coming months with the next Grand Slam tournament the French Open from late May to early June.

articles.text: Hikers and mountain bikers often love the same trails. But sometimes that love can lead to tension, such as when a biker approaches without warning and a collision is narrowly avoided. As a Scout in Piedmont Troop 15, Schuyler Sawicki knew he wanted to do his Eagle service project at nearby Joaquin Miller Park where he loves to ride his bike and train for the Piedmont Mountain Bike Team. He approached a conservation group, The Friends of Joaquin Miller Park, for ideas. It led to an initiative suggested by the Bicycle Trails Council of the East Bay – building a bike bell kiosk. On Saturday, January 21, Sawicki led a crew of Scouts and mountain bike team members in constructing two bike bell kiosks at the park, encouraging mountain bikers to borrow a ball for their rides. The bike bells provide hikers with an early warning of oncoming bikers and are a common trait for several local trails. opportunity to borrow a bell, the goal of the kiosk is to increase bell usage and educate mountain bikers about their benefits. “I love it when I can hear people on bikes racing down the hill. Sharing the road is not a concept for many bikers. Thank you for providing bells for riders,” marveled local hiker, Margaret Charnas. Sawicki first gained approval for the project by presenting it to the City of Oakland’s Parks and Recreation Commission, which eventually approved it. He then set up a GoFundMe page and raised enough to pay for building materials, signs, and attachable bike bells. Many of his donors are from the mountain bike community. In addition, Economy Lumber agreed to donate material for the kiosk. Bikers are asked to return the bell to the kiosk or make a donation to the BTCEB to support replacement bells. The bike bell kiosks that Sawicki and friends installed at Joaquin Miller are in two locations, one near the meadow on the approach to Sunset Trail, and the other just off Skyline Road at the start of the Palos Colorados and Sequoia-Bayview trails. “I just want bikers to realize how much of an impact they can have in bettering the community through riding with a bell and being friendly to other trail users. I want everyone to have a good experience in the park,” said Sawicki. Piedmont Mountain Bike Team is very proud of Sawicki’s work and is excited to see how his project is received by the community. By Jonathan Comeaux Mackie McDonald put up a battle but lost in the third round of the Australian Open to No. 31 seed Yoshihito Nishioka on Thursday, January 19 in three sets, 7-6 (8-6), 6-3, 6-2. Regardless of the exit for McDonald, he walked out of the Grand Slam after pulling off the biggest win of his professional career when defeating Rafael Nadal in three sets a week ago on January 17. McDonald reflected on his win over Nadal and how the Spanish legend dealt with a nagging hip injury late in the match. “I’m really happy with how I started that match, I thought I was playing really well, serving great, and returning well too. I was really taking it to him. But I hated to see him (injured) in the third set. It was pretty tough to stay mentally engaged, but I just found a way to pull it out,” said McDonald. McDonald admitted that he got out of rhythm after Nadal suffered his injury. “He’s an incredible champion, he’s never going to give up regardless of the situation, so even closing it out against a top guy like that is always tough. I was trying to stay focused on what I was doing and he got me out of rhythm with that. I’m happy that I just kept focusing on myself in the end and got through,” said McDonald. Regardless of Nadal’s injury, McDonald played steady throughout the match and he’s aware just how on top of his game he was on that Wednesday morning in Melbourne. McDonald has always been best on the hard courts and feels he had the “guns” to keep up with the former champion. “I think I have the guns to do it. I was blasting the ball, hitting really flat. Last time I played him, he kicked my butt. On clay courts, it’s tough to hit through, but here I like my chances on hard courts. I really wanted to take it to him on a hard court, I happy I got that opportunity and got away with it,” said McDonald. Former Piedmont coach Neil Rothenberg, who coached McDonald when he was a student at Piedmont High School, made an appearance on ABC7 News to talk about Mackie. “It was awesome to watch it. You’re always on pins and needles, especially when you’re playing one of the greatest players of all time. After the first set, you always get nervous and ask ‘Can he win the second set?’ and then it became, ‘Well, can he actually win the match?’ He has a lot of fans in Piedmont, we were all communicating with each other,” said Rothenberg. “I don’t think I’ve ever seen him play as well as he did and I’ve known him since he was seven years old. He would go to some of the clinics that pros would hold and he was always involved as one of the participants. You could tell even at seven- and eight-years old that he had an unbelievable amount of presence. We were just hoping that when he got to high school that he would play for Piedmont because it’s very unusual to have a world class player play high school tennis,” said Rothenberg. We’ll cover McDonald once again in the coming months with the next Grand Slam tournament the French Open from late May to early June.

The speaker event showcases women’s storytelling in poetry, music, and the art of flower arranging. All speaker events are free with Filoli admission; however, a reservation is required to attend due to limited space. articles.text: Michelle Williams and Ryan Gosling in Blue Valentine It’s not uncommon to hear a film praised for being unflinchingly honest, even stark. But embedded in that praise is the question: how close to life do audiences really want their movies to be? That is the dilemma inherent in Blue Valentine. Essentially, it takes what might be called a romance and juxtaposes it with life six years later. The film opens in real time with Dean (Ryan Gosling) and Cindy (Michelle Williams) and their little girl, Frankie (Faith Wladyka), living in a modest house in Scranton, PA. Dean paints houses and Cindy is a nurse. Life has intruded, leeching the joy out of their relationship, and burnishing all the spontaneity from their marriage. Cindy is bone tired and deeply discontent. Dean seems oblivious to her personal struggle. articles.text: Amandla Stenberg and Nick Robinson star in Everything, Everything. Everything, Everything is a sweet teen movie that will have special appeal to young girls. It’s reminiscent of countless stories of forbidden love, which makes it familiar, universal, and, of course, hugely sentimental. The basic set up: A girl, Maddy (Amandla Stenberg), on the cusp of her 18th birthday, looks out at the world through walls of glass. Since infancy she has grown up trapped in her hermetically sealed home, unable to venture outside lest she become lethally ill. Her diagnosis: severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). Maddy, standing in front of the countess windows, dreams of running along beaches, floating in the ocean or walking along a residential street. Her mother is a doctor and treats her illness while the two of them live in a beautiful, modern upscale house designed to protect Maddy. One spring day, new people move in next door, to include an 18-year-old boy, Olly (Nick Robinson), a skateboarder who, standing by the moving truck, looks up and sees Maddy looking down at him from her wide window. He is intrigued; she is captivated. They tentatively wave hello. As it turns out their bedroom windows are across a narrow walkway and gradually they watch each other, then begin to text, talk and grow close, all within the parameters of what she can and cannot do, meaning for any reason she can’t go past the front door. Of course, this is a love story, so Maddy and Olly find a way. And finally, given permission by Maddy’s nurse, Carla (Ana De La Reguera), Olly is allowed inside the house, as long as he keeps his distance and definitely no touching. To tell any more about the plot would be unfair. Suffice it to say that Stenberg and Robinson are perfectly matched and exude chemistry. There is a deep innocence about their connection and the fact that Maddy has been sheltered from the world only contributes to what will be an overwhelming sense of awe once she risks everything to be with Olly. Teenagers, the target audience, will love this movie. Everything, Everything. Directed by Stella Meghie. Starring Amandla Stenberg, Nick Robinson and Ana De La Reguera. 1 hr., 36 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2017. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: One of Disney’s favorite tropes has been the adorable princess and the wicked stepmother. Recall Snow White and the spiked apple; Cinderella, forced to scrub and clean; or Rapunzel, locked away in a high tower. Pixar’s contribution, Brave, does feature a strong-willed teenage princess, Merida (Kelly MacDonald), who rebels not against an unkind stepmother, but against her imperious mother, queen Elinor (Emma Thompson). The period is medieval Scotland, filled with crags and castles and rolling highlands. And there is, of course, Merida, with her massive ginger-colored tresses, a young royal who happens to identify with her father, onelegged, big lug King Fergus (Bill Connoly). She can ride like the wind and is an expert archer (not unlike Katniss Everdeen of The Hunger Games). She would rather be racing horseback through the surrounding forests than spending time with the staid ladies of the court. Elinor, of course, has her own ideas of how a young princess should behave. But Merida, as wild as her red mane, snorts when she laughs, scoops up food from the pantry, and is a tomboyish, headstrong teenager who has her own ideas regarding gender equality. Queen Elinor is not to be deterred in her efforts to civilize Merida in the image of a proper princess, marriage being at the fore. She therefore invites three suitors to the yearly Highland Games, deciding that the best of the three will win her daughter’s hand. Merida, of course, has other plans. She finds all three definitely unsuitable as prospective husbands, and declares to her mother that she’ll not marry, period, followed by an age-appropriate tantrum to make her point. To further drive home wishes to be her own person, she dominates the archery contest with extraordinary skill and accuracy. But when her mother insists that she will accept the best suitor, Merida runs away into the forest. To her surprise she comes upon a cottage inhabited by an old witch, a crone with magical powers who tells the princess that she can, indeed, cast a spell on Elinor. Merida rashly, rebelliously, agrees. She realizes, too late, however, that her decision has some unintended consequences. In other words, be careful what you wish for when you say, “I want my freedom!” Brave, has more than a few Disneyesque life lessons that result in some tender moments between daughter and mother. This is a wonderfully animated tale that is easy to like. And it’s Pixar’s first female lead out of 13 feature films. Brave. Pixar animation. Directed by Mark Andrews and Brenda Chapman. With voices of Kelly MacDonald, Bill Connoly, Emma Thompson. 1 hr., 33 min. Rated PG. Released 2012. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Disney+.

articles.text: Piedmont cartoonist Philip Witte, creator of the Flip cartoons that appear weekly in the Piedmont Post, nationally in the New Yorker and Wall Street Journal, and internationally throughout the UK including Galway, Ireland, is having an exhibit of selected works at Piedmont Center for the Arts from now through February 5. Gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays. A bit of background Since leaving his legal career seven years ago, Piedmonter Phil Witte has sold more than 1,000 cartoons to dozens of publications in the U.S., U.K., and Galway, Ireland. A cartoonist from an early age, once he began his studies at Princeton he abandoned cartooning. Following some time working in Bangkok, he entered law school at the University of Chicago. Although life as a litigation attorney was all-consuming, Phil tried to find time for creative activities. He wrote a few humor pieces, which attracted the attention of a book publisher. That led to a joke book, What You Don’t Know About Turning 50, and a sequel on turning 60. Sales to date are approaching 175,000 copies. “I knew I could write jokes, so I figured if I could combine that with drawing, I could become a cartoonist,” he said. “I was decent in art, but I needed to get a lot better, plus I had to develop a style… I’m still working on that.” He showed his early work to Phil Frank, the late cartoonist at The San Francisco Chronicle, who encouraged him. While work on his art, Witte collaborated as a gag writer for syndicated cartoonists, including Dan Piraro, creator of the cartoon feature “Bizarro.” Phil has 25 original ink drawings by Piraro Yorker, who hired them to write a bi-monthly blog called “Anatomy of a Cartoon” for the CartoonStock site (cartoonstock.com), resulting in almost 100 posts and counting. After trying for years to place his cartoons in The New Yorker, he decided to collaborate with one of the magazine’s veteran cartoonists, Kaamran Hafeez. “I sent him hundreds of gags over the past couple of years. He drew 50 or so of them and submitted them with his own cartoons.” Last year, two of them were published in The New Yorker. Even most of the “regular” cartoonists at the magazine get their work rejected over 95 percent of the time, Phil noted. Witte was recently elected by his peers to the National Cartoonist Society. His cartoons have been exhibited in San Francisco, Oakland, Minneapolis, London, Galway, Ireland, and most recently at Dominican University in San Rafael. His show at the Piedmont Center for the Arts will include cartoons from the Dominican show, plus a few new cartoons. He has been a guest cartoonist at the Cartoon Art Museum in San Francisco and the Charles Schulz Museum in Santa Rosa. There is even a museum of cartoon art in Bulgaria that has one of his cartoons in their permanent collection. articles.text: Cassoulet is a classic French dish which is especially enjoyable during cold winter months. It has a reputation for being very difficult to make, but here is a version that is easy as can be. I have provided a number of variations to make it even simpler. The classic cassoulet is made with white beans and a variety of flavorful meats. The usual recipe uses duck, bacon, and sausage for the meats. This is combined with white beans, leeks, herbs, and some white wine. This recipe will serve two. Preheat the oven to 275°. It is best to use a cast-iron skillet. Put a tablespoon of olive oil in the pan. Mince one carrot, one stalk of celery, one shallot or half an onion, a leek, and some garlic. Put into the skillet to brown and add about a tablespoon of whole peppercorns, some French herbs, a healthy squeeze of tomato paste and anchovy paste. If you want the classic, use one can of white beans. Spaniards would use a can of garbanzos. Put these on top of your browned, vegetables, and top with some breadcrumbs. For the meats my first choice is duck confit, one duck leg per person. Add any of your favorite sausage. Other meats that could be used are fresh chicken legs, or turkey. Put the meat on top of your vegetables and pop in the oven for at least one hour. Add white wine to taste.

articles.text: I am periodically asked how I knew I wanted to become an architect. My journey to becoming an architect is grounded both in certain proclivities that I had in my nature as well as other interests that were developed through my early interactions with my family. Serendipity also played a large role in my choosing this professional path. I grew up in a family that had some creative talent (my mother and older brother had artistic skills), but everyone in the family had little interest in fix-it repairs. If something was broken and needed fixing, I became the go-to guy at any early age. I had no fear about taking apart something that was broken, and was fascinated by how things worked, how they were put together. Many times, I couldn’t get things back together, but there were many successes when I found the root of the problem and reconstructed things in a working order. My parents empowered me to develop those skills. I also enjoyed watching my mother and brother doing their artwork, which mostly consisted of sketching and oil painting. I would steal my brother’s paint and make my own paintings. In high school I was a decent art student, but I gravitated to the wood shop, metal shop, and automotive repair classes. When it came time to apply for colleges I decided that engineering would be right for me. Just before dropping the application into the mailbox, I had a second thought, I was also interested in making art, so at the last minute I changed my application to the architectural program. That last-minute decision was fortuitous, as I have never regretted it. It hasn’t always been an easy path, but it has definitely been a fulfilling one. Edward Kaplan AIA, NCARB, is principal of Kaplan Architects in Oakland and San Francisco since 1985. articles.text: Dear Jim: I need your help. My basement flooded with 6 inches of water this year after it has been dry for the 30 years we have lived here. I’m assuming multiple atmospheric rivers got this started. We had an old sump pump in place and had plumbers come and install 2 more during this recent series of storms, but they don’t help at all. What should I do? The sump pump can be a lifesaver in the correct application. Unfortunately, it is not an effective tool for most of the drainage problems we experience in the Bay Area, which are accelerating with climate change and are demanding a more comprehensive approach. What a Sump Pump is good for A sump pump is primarily useful for removing localized surface water inside your home in the location it is placed, or at the exterior as part of a drainage system to pump water to the street. If you have water on the floor in a furnace room the sump pump will remove the bulk of the standing water. If you have a crawlspace or basement where water is being channeled to a specific location, the sump pump may help. A sump pump will generally only remove underground water in relationship to its depth- i.e. a sump well which is 2’ deep will normally remove water that gets within 2 feet of it. Why Sump Pumps are generally ineffective Unfortunately, our clay soils do not allow water to flow very well laterally. Translated this means the water that is migrating under our foundations will not be able to find the sump pump unless it is directed there. Subterranean water is frequently traveling under our foundations and popping up downstream in our crawlspaces or basements at various locations, and these locations can change as soils expand and contract in relationship to wet and dry conditions and vary with storms coming from different directions. A sump pump may seem like it is working because it sits in a hole below the water table causing it to fill up with water, but that may not be the water you need to get rid of. What is the Answer? The answer is to install a proper drainage system, sometimes expensive, never fun, always time consuming, but very effective (if done correctly). A well-designed combination of French Drains and downspout drainage will protect the perimeter of your home and never allow water to get to those locations that are getting flooded, channeling water away from your house. In effect, we would be putting a moat around your home to protect it. Water does not belong under your house and can lead to settlement, foundation damage and structural issues that can lead to costly repairs. Now may be the time to consider how to best protect what is likely your most valuable financial investment. Foundations exposed to significant long-term moisture eventually fail. articles.text: Mary Rickard was a Piedmont resident from 2009 to 2020. Former Piedmont resident Mary Kathryn Rickard passed away unexpectedly on January 9, 2023, near her home in Fall City, Washington. Born in Waterloo, Iowa on July 22, 1962, she graduated from the University of Northern Iowa and moved to the Bay Area, where she met her husband Graham Rickard. After a courtship that spanned a few years and several cities, they wed in London in January, 1998. After living in London, Detroit, and Alameda, they moved to Piedmont in 2009. Their family included two beautiful children, Alex and Zoë, who both graduated from Piedmont High School. Two years ago, as empty nesters, Mary and Graham moved to Fall City to begin their next adventure. Mary loved the beauty, space, verdant landscape, and warm community there. She took great joy in mowing the lawn, planning for her summer garden, cultivating fruit trees, keeping an eye on the local bear, and helping Graham with his beekeeping. She kept in close contact with her family and friends around the world, checking in often and visiting regularly. Mary loved hiking, biking, knitting/sewing, Scrabble, the New York Times crossword puzzle, Bruce Springsteen, Jack Nicklaus, Tiger Woods, the Giants, and the Warriors. She was a wonderful wife, mother, daughter, sister, and friend, with a tremendous sense of loyalty and a delightful sense of humor. Her family and friends are grateful that she passed with a heart overflowing with love and a soul filled with life’s greatest experiences. While we will miss her forever, she will live on in all of us. Mary was a great believer in the power of public service and community. In lieu of flowers, please make donations to Habitat for Humanity, one of Mary’s favorite organizations. “If I had a flower for every time I thought of you . . . I could walk in my garden forever.” –Alfred Lord Tennyson

articles.text: A strong turnout of 18 readers showed up at Piedmont Community Hall for the First Monday reading group in January for a discussion of Afterparties. On hand were Bob and Madeline Hall, Adrienne Hamlin, Ken Young, Darby and Gerry Gragg, Mike Bandrowski, Phil Witte, Martin Levy, Dick Carter, Bella Almanzan, Albert Chen, Melba Yee, Mike Henn, Sarah Johnson, and discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. Afterparties is the highly acclaimed debut collection of short stories by Anthony Veasna So, who died in 2020 at age 28 from a drug overdose. He was a young, queer, Cambodian American who wrote about issues associated with his ethnic Khmer identity and sexuality. The book was named a “Best Book of the Year” by the New York Times, National Public Radio, the Washington Post, the Loa Angeles Times, and others. Reader Darby Gragg shared that the book is required reading for her grandson’s college gender studies course. Afterparties is a set of stories about Cambodian-American life in America. The book is comic, but intense, and sexually graphic, providing insight into the life of queer and immigrant communities. The primary characters are often the children of refugees who suffered terrible trauma during the Cambodian Genocide, where 25% of the population was killed. These parents later created lives for themselves and their children in the Central Valley of California. In Afterparties these young people grapple with race, sexuality, friendship, and family in a place where their vocational options often came down to fixing cars, selling donuts, or going on welfare. So’s stories include two drunken brothers who attend a wedding afterparty and decide to expose their shady uncle’s snubbing of the bride and groom, and a high school badminton coach who tries to relive his glory days by beating a rising teenage star. There’s also a love affair between an older tech entrepreneur and a disillusioned, young teacher. In the final story, a nine-year-old child learns that his mother survived a racist school shooter. The book generated strong positive responses from most of the group. They felt So was an extremely talented writer, who wrote powerfully, creatively, and beautifully. His writing style was also crisp, fast, direct, raw, and impactful. He wrote as if he was talking directly with his readers, but tragically died at a very young age, and thus deprived them of his future works. So’s characters are rich in detail, and they reflect their immigrant families’ stressful experiences; which some readers could personally relate to. The generational effect of the genocide on the survivors and especially the children is evident and important to realize. Some members of the group had read nothing before about Cambodian refugees in the Central Valley, so the book provided this understanding too. It was noted that So was bipolar and could have periods of creative brilliance, but also falling-off-the-cliff depression. The cause behind So’s overdose death is unknown. However, there were readers who were less enthusiastic about the book. Some liked some of the stories, but not all of them. Some didn’t like his treatment of the Cambodian American culture, and questions were raised about how So’s community feels about the book. Still others found his detailed descriptions of gay sex more than they wanted to know. The situations of the characters were also depressing for some, and this led to an interesting discussion of the responsibilities of the writer and the reader. It was asked if a writer has an obligation to provide something positive for the readers, or is it the reader’s responsibility to make the effort to understand what the writer is trying to share? It was accepted that each reader bring her/his own baggage to a book that can determine if the book is enjoyed, but it was also said that well-written works are always exhilarating. Afterparties provided an understanding of experiences and a culture previously unknown to most of the readers, and this was appreciated. Additionally, readers agreed this was a book they would not have read if not for the First Mondays Reading Group, and they benefited from it. With their discussion complete the group considered their next books. They try to alternate fiction and non-fiction. They had previously selected Prisoners of Geography: Ten Maps that Explain Everything About the World, by Tim Marshall for February, and The Buddha in the Attic, a 2011 novel by American author Julie Otsuka, for March. pages.text: Wednesday, January 25, 2023 23 First Monday Readers tackle Afterparties By Dick Carter A strong turnout of 18 readers showed up at Piedmont Community Hall for the First Monday reading group in January for a discussion of Afterparties. On hand were Bob and Madeline Hall, Adrienne Hamlin, Ken Young, Darby and Gerry Gragg, Mike Bandrowski, Phil Witte, Martin Levy, Dick Carter, Bella Almanzan, Albert Chen, Melba Yee, Mike Henn, Sarah Johnson, and discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. Afterparties is the highly acclaimed debut collection of short stories by Anthony Veasna So, who died in 2020 at age 28 from a drug overdose. He was a young, queer, Cambodian American who wrote about issues associated with his ethnic Khmer identity and sexuality. The book was named a “Best Book of the Year” by the New York Times, National Public Radio, the Washington Post, the Loa Angeles Times, and others. Reader Darby Gragg shared that the book is required reading for her grandson’s college gender studies course. Afterparties is a set of stories about Cambodian-American life in America. The book is comic, but intense, and sexually graphic, providing insight into the life of queer and immigrant communities. The primary characters are often the children of refugees who suffered terrible trauma during the Cambodian Genocide, where 25% of the population was killed. These parents later created lives for themselves and their children in the Central Valley of California. In Afterparties these young people grapple with race, sexuality, friendship, and family in a place where their vocational options often came down to fixing cars, selling donuts, or going on welfare. So’s stories include two drunken brothers who attend a wedding afterparty and decide to expose their shady uncle’s snubbing of the bride and groom, and a high school badminton coach who tries to relive his glory days by beating a rising teenage star. There’s also a love affair between an older tech entrepreneur and a disillusioned, young teacher. In the final story, a nine-year-old child learns that his mother survived a racist school shooter. The book generated strong positive responses from most of the group. They felt So was an extremely talented writer, who wrote powerfully, creatively, and beautifully. His writing style was also crisp, fast, direct, raw, and impactful. He wrote as if he was talking directly with his readers, but tragically died at a very young age, and thus deprived them of his future works. So’s characters are rich in detail, and they reflect their immigrant families’ stressful experiences; which some readers could personally relate to. The generational effect of the genocide on the survivors and especially the children is evident and important to realize. Some members of the group had read nothing before about Cambodian refugees in the Central Valley, so the book provided this understanding too. It was noted that So was bipolar and could have periods of creative brilliance, but also falling-off-the-cliff depression. The cause behind So’s overdose death is unknown. However, there were readers who were less enthusiastic about the book. Some liked some of the stories, but not all of them. Some didn’t like his treatment of the Cambodian American culture, and questions were raised about how So’s community feels about the book. Still others found his detailed descriptions of gay sex more than they wanted to know. The situations of the characters were also depressing for some, and this led to an interesting discussion of the responsibilities of the writer and the reader. It was asked if a writer has an obligation to provide something positive for the readers, or is it the reader’s responsibility to make the effort to understand what the writer is trying to share? It was accepted that each reader bring her/his own baggage to a book that can determine if the book is enjoyed, but it was also said that well-written works are always exhilarating. Afterparties provided an understanding of experiences and a culture previously unknown to most of the readers, and this was appreciated. Additionally, readers agreed this was a book they would not have read if not for the First Mondays Reading Group, and they benefited from it. With their discussion complete the group considered their next books. They try to alternate fiction and non-fiction. They had previously selected Prisoners of Geography: Ten Maps that Explain Everything About the World, by Tim Marshall for February, and The Buddha in the Attic, a 2011 novel by American author Julie Otsuka, for March. For April the group selected Trevor Noah’s memoir Born a Crime. Former Piedmont resident Mary Kathryn Rickard passed away unexpectedly on January 9, 2023, near her home in Fall City, Washington. Born in Waterloo, Iowa on July 22, 1962, she graduated from the University of Northern Iowa and moved to the Bay Area, where she met her husband Graham Rickard. After a courtship that spanned a few years and several cities, they wed in London in January, 1998. After living in London, Detroit, and Alameda, they moved to Piedmont in 2009. Their family included two beautiful children, Alex and Zoë, who both graduated from Piedmont High School. Two years ago, as empty nesters, Mary and Graham moved to Fall City to begin their next adventure. Mary loved the beauty, space, verdant landscape, and warm community there. She took great joy in mowing the lawn, planning for her summer garden, cultivating fruit trees, keeping an eye on the local bear, and helping Graham with his beekeeping. She kept in close contact with her family and friends around the world, checking in often and visiting regularly. Mary loved hiking, biking, knitting/sewing, Scrabble, the New York Times crossword puzzle, Bruce Springsteen, Jack Nicklaus, Tiger Woods, the Giants, and the Warriors. She was a wonderful wife, mother, daughter, sister, and friend, with a tremendous sense of loyalty and a delightful sense of humor. Her family and friends are grateful that she passed with a heart overflowing with love and a soul filled with life’s greatest experiences. While we will miss her forever, she will live on in all of us. Mary was a great believer in the power of public service and community. The Overstory: A Novel by Richard Powers The Overstory, winner of the 2019 Pulitzer Prize in Fiction, is a sweeping, impassioned work of activism and resistance that is also a stunning evocation of the natural world. From the roots to the crown and back to the seeds, Richard Powers’ twelfth novel unfolds in concentric rings of interlocking fables that range from antebellum New York to the late twentieth-century Timber Wars of the Pacific Northwest and beyond. There is a world alongside ours ― vast, slow, interconnected, resourceful, magnificently inventive, and almost invisible to us. This is the story of a handful of people who learn how to see that world and who are drawn up into its unfolding catastrophe.” Sophie Roberts is a Climate Corps Fellow with the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division. Contact her at sroberts@ piedmont.ca.gov with questions on electrification, plant-based eating, or hiking. 5. Merchants of Doubt: How a Handful of Scientists Obscured the Truth on Issues from Tobacco Smoke to Global Warming by Naomi Oreskes and Erik M. Conway “Merchants of Doubt has been praised and attacked around the world for reasons easy to understand. This book tells the disquieting story of how a loose-knit group of high-level scientists and scientific advisers, with deep connections in politics and industry, ran effective campaigns to mislead the public and deny well-established scientific knowledge for more than four decades. The same individuals who claim the science of global warming is ‘not settled’ have also denied the truth about studies linking smoking to lung cancer, coal smoke to acid rain, and CFCs to the ozone hole. ‘Doubt is our product,’ wrote one tobacco executive. These ‘experts’ supplied it. Merchants of Doubt rolls back the rug on this dark corner of American science.” The portrayals are superb. Michele Williams is stunning as Cindy. And Ryan Gosling captures Dean perfectly. These are fine actors who bring to bear all of their talent. Director Derek Cianfrance, with cinematographer Andrij Parekh, shot the flashbacks in 16-mm, creating a softness to their courtship. Real time scenes are shot in digital, giving them a crisp, almost flat look, with less depth and color. Though the audience may not be aware of the difference, most filmmakers will insist that the message is the medium, so to speak. This is a film that is provocative, engaging, and is far from the happy meal being served up by Hollywood. Hopefully, it will find an audience Blue Valentine. Directed by Derek Cianfrance. Starring Ryan Gosling, Michelle Williams, John Donan and Faith Wladyka. 2 hrs. Rated R. Streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: Automatic license plate readers at Moraga and Ramona Avenues were triggered by a stolen black 2020 Hyundai Elantra on January 16 shortly after 11 a.m. The vehicle was stolen in Oakland on December 31. A Piedmont police officer located the vehicle parked on the second story of the Rockridge Safeway parking lot at 5100 Broadway. After activating his emergency lights the officer observed a woman in the front passenger seat. As the officer went to the vehicle, the woman reached over and locked the vehicle. She then moved over to the driver’s seat and used pliers to start the vehicle. The officer broke out the driver side window with a baton in attempt to detain the occupant before she fled. The occupant then quickly reversed the vehicle into the patrol vehicle with the officer nearby and proceeded to flee at high speed. Piedmont Police Sgt. Wright authorized a pursuit of the vehicle. The suspect collided with a pole and a red 2018 Lexus ES300 in the area of Broadway and Coronado Avenue in Oakland. The driver got out of the vehicle and fled on foot on Broadway towards Pleasant Valley Avenue. Officers were able to detain the driver and place her under arrest. A Piedmont police officer located the vehicle parked on the second story of the Rockridge Safeway parking lot at 5100 Broadway. The occupant then quickly reversed the vehicle into the patrol vehicle with the officer nearby and proceeded to flee at high speed. Piedmont Police Sgt. Wright authorized a pursuit of the vehicle.
